title: Sleep Disorders: Insomnia Management with Circadian Rhythm–Focused Strategies
summary: Insomnia is common and frequently intertwined with circadian rhythm misalignment. First-line therapy is CBT‑I, with targeted circadian interventions—timed light, melatonin/melatonin agonists, and structured sleep scheduling—used when delayed or advanced sleep-wake phase, jet lag, or shift work features are present. Pharmacologic options have comparative evidence for short- and long-term insomnia control, but should be integrated with circadian optimization to sustain benefits and reduce adverse effects.
clinicalQuestion: What are evidence-based strategies to manage insomnia with a focus on circadian rhythm assessment and correction?

keyMoments.title: Prioritize circadian assessment
keyMoments.body: Identify phase delay vs advance using sleep logs/actigraphy and social/work constraints; target phase with light and melatonin timing for maximal phase-shift efficacy [3], [4], [5].

keyMoments.title: Combine CBT‑I with circadian therapy
keyMoments.body: CBT‑I remains first-line for insomnia; adding properly timed light and melatonin addresses misalignment and enhances durability of sleep improvements [3], [6], [7].

keyMoments.title: Use melatonin precisely
keyMoments.body: Small evening doses to advance delayed rhythms or morning doses to delay advanced rhythms; timing relative to dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) determines direction of shift [8], [4], [5].

keyMoments.title: Match light to the goal
keyMoments.body: Morning bright light to advance; evening bright light to delay. Control competing light exposure (blue-light avoidance at undesired phase) to prevent counter-shifts [3], [8], [7].

keyMoments.title: Choose medications judiciously
keyMoments.body: Network meta-analysis shows differing benefit–risk profiles across hypnotics; consider long-term balance of efficacy, safety, and dependence risk and always integrate circadian care [9].

sections.title: Stepwise Management of Insomnia with Circadian Focus
sections.blurb: A structured approach integrates diagnosis, circadian phase targeting, behavioral therapy, and selective pharmacotherapy.

steps.title: Screen and phenotype
steps.body: Use sleep diaries (≥2 weeks), actigraphy if available, and work/school timing to determine delayed vs advanced phase, shift work, or jet lag patterns. Identify perpetuating factors for CBT‑I and comorbidities (psychiatric/medical) that interact with circadian timing [3], [7], [2].

steps.title: Implement CBT‑I core
steps.body: Apply sleep restriction, stimulus control, and cognitive strategies; reinforce regular wake time and time-in-bed titration. CBT‑I is the **foundation** for chronic insomnia; pair with circadian tools for misalignment [6], [7].

steps.title: Target circadian phase with light
steps.body: For delayed sleep-wake: deliver **morning bright light** (2,500–10,000 lux for 30–60 min) and reduce evening blue light; for advanced phase: apply **evening bright light** and protect morning light exposure to delay timing [3], [8], [4], [7].

steps.title: Add timed melatonin or agonists
steps.body: For phase advance (DSWPD): **low-dose melatonin (0.3–1 mg) 4–8 h before habitual bedtime** or ~5–6 h before DLMO; for phase delay (ASWPD/early awakenings): consider **morning melatonin** in low dose to delay. Melatonin receptor agonists may aid entrainment and insomnia symptoms [8], [4], [5], [6].

steps.title: Optimize sleep scheduling
steps.body: Institute fixed wake time; anchor light exposure to the target schedule. Consider chronotherapy (progressive delay) cautiously and under supervision for severe DSWPD; avoid relapse by maintaining zeitgeber regularity [10], [4], [5].

steps.title: Pharmacologic insomnia options
steps.body: If needed, select agents with favorable long-term profiles per network meta-analysis, balancing benefits and adverse events. Always combine with CBT‑I and circadian alignment to limit dose/duration and prevent rebound [9].

steps.title: Relapse prevention and follow-up
steps.body: Maintain regular light/dark cues, consistent rise time, and device-light hygiene. Reassess phase and sleep efficiency; taper hypnotics when stable. Address comorbid depression/anxiety where circadian therapies may confer additional benefit [6], [7].

sections.title: Protocols, Dosing, and Safety
sections.blurb: Actionable circadian and insomnia interventions with timing emphasis.

cards.title: Bright light therapy
items: Goal advance (DSWPD/late sleep): **Morning light** 30–60 min at 2,500–10,000 lux; avoid evening blue light [3], [8], [4], [7].
Goal delay (ASWPD/early awakenings): **Evening light** 30–60 min; limit early-morning light with sunglasses if outdoors [3], [7].
Device light hygiene: blue-light filters, dim lights 2–3 h before target bedtime; maximize post-wake light.
Cautions: migraine, bipolar spectrum (monitor activation), retinal disease—coordinate with ophthalmology if needed [3].

cards.title: Melatonin and agonists
items: **Advance** timing: 0.3–1 mg 4–8 h before habitual bedtime (≈5–6 h before DLMO) for DSWPD; higher doses do not increase phase shift and may cause sleepiness [8], [4], [5].
**Delay** timing: low-dose morning melatonin for ASWPD; avoid evening dosing in advanced phase.
Agonists: consider ramelteon or melatonin agonists when insomnia plus CRSWD or mood disorders are present [6].
Safety: daytime sedation, interaction with anticoagulants; standardize brand/formulation to reduce variability.

cards.title: CBT‑I essentials
items: Sleep restriction to consolidate sleep; titrate by weekly sleep efficiency.
Stimulus control: bed only for sleep; leave bed if awake >15–20 min.
Cognitive work: reframe catastrophic sleep beliefs; paradoxical intention for sleep effort.
Relapse plan: protect wake time, travel/shift protocols, and light exposure anchors [7].

cards.title: Shift work & jet lag
items: Shift work: phase-directional light blocks at work vs commute; strategic naps; caffeine early in shift; melatonin for daytime sleep facilitation as appropriate [3], [7].
Jet lag: eastward—advance pre-trip with earlier sleep, **morning destination light** and pre-sleep melatonin; westward—delay schedule with **evening light** at destination [3], [11].
Protect circadian cues: consistent meals, exercise timing aligned to target phase.

cards.title: Pharmacologic insomnia options
items: Network meta-analysis: differing short- vs long-term efficacy and harms; tailor to age/comorbidity and minimize duration [9].
Avoid routine antipsychotics or strong anticholinergics for insomnia; monitor for falls, cognitive effects in older adults.
Always pair with circadian measures to reduce dose and prevent dependence.

cards.title: When to refer
items: Refractory DSWPD/ASWPD requiring chronotherapy or DLMO measurement.
Complex comorbidity (bipolar disorder, severe ocular disease).
Suspected comorbid sleep apnea, RLS/PLMD, or parasomnias complicating insomnia.
